content: This condition was most prevalent among individuals employed in the matchstick manufacturing industry during the 19th and early 20th centuries. Advances in industrial hygiene have since eradicated the circumstances that led to this disease. Chronic inhalation of white phosphorus vapors, which were a key component in the production of matches from the 1840s to the 1910s, resulted in the accumulation of phosphorus in the jawbones. Workers initially experienced intense toothaches and gum swelling. Over time, the jawbone would develop abscesses, leading to excruciating pain and severe disfigurement. The condition was further characterized by the emission of a putrid odor from the necrotic bone tissue, which made the affected individuals socially ostracized. In advanced stages, the jawbones would decay and emit a greenish-white phosphorescent glow in the dark. At this critical stage, surgical removal of the affected jawbone was often the only intervention that could potentially save the patient’s life. Without such intervention, the disease would progress to systemic organ failure, ultimately resulting in death. Public outrage over the horrific nature of this condition eventually led to reforms in match production processes, effectively eliminating the disease. A similar condition, known as osteonecrosis of the jaw, has been identified as a rare but serious side effect of bisphosphonates. These are phosphorus-based medications widely used to treat osteoporosis, bone metastases in cancer, and other bone-related disorders. Bisphosphonates work by inhibiting bone resorption, but in some cases, they can lead to necrosis of the jawbone.
